newsitem.title: SPAIN: Catalans close to backing Spanish budget - Molins.
newsitem.headline: Catalans close to backing Spanish budget - Molins.

text.p: The difference of opinion between the Spanish government and its Catalan allies over next year's budget is small and can be overcome, Catalan parliamentary spokesman Joaquim Molins said in an interview published on Sunday.
"It (the difference) is no more than 100 or 150 billion pesetas ($800 million to $1.2 billion). It's not a problem," Molins told the daily El Pais.
The major area of discrepancy between the minority Popular Party (PP) government and the Catalans, whose support is vital to passing a budget, is over health spending.
The budget, the key to Spain's chances of joining a single European currency in 1999, is widely seen as the four-month-old government's biggest test so far.
Overall spending on health has to rise to close the gap with other European countries, the Catalan nationalist coalition CiU (Convergence and Unity) says.

But Molins said the Catalans would accept an initial reduction of around 110 billion pesetas in health spending if it were then compensated with savings made in other areas -- specifically a public sector salary freeze and possible charges for prescriptions.

A real growth forecast of three percent next year (six percent nominal growth assuming three percent inflation) and expectations of extra income from new taxes, like a charge on risk insurance, imply revenues could increase by an extra 300 billion pesetas on top of the original 400 billion estimate, Molins said.
The cost cuts pending are still around 500 billion pesetas, he added.
This compares with total central government spending in the draft 1996 budget of nearly 30 trillion pesetas.

Asked if he thought three percent GDP growth next year was over-optimistic, Molins noted the OECD forecast was 2.6 to 2.7 percent but said he personally was more optimistic than he had been three months ago that Spain could achieve three percent.
"It all depends on the last quarter," he said.
The economy grew by an estimated 1.9 percent in the first half of this year (definitive second quarter figures have yet to be released) and is expected to pick up in the second half.
